opus-5.5.text:
I think luck plays a much bigger role than most people like to admit, including the parts we usually credit to ourselves, like being hardworking or driven.

When people see someone who works very hard, they often say, "That's discipline, that's character." And sure, there's some choice involved. But if I'm honest, a lot of my ability to stay hungry came from things I didn't choose. I happened to find something I genuinely love, which is building things with computers, graphics, and simulation, quite early. When you love something, working hard doesn't feel like sacrifice. It feels like playing. I didn't earn that; I was lucky to stumble into it.

I was also lucky to have people around me at the right moments: teachers who tolerated my weird side projects, advisors who gave me freedom, collaborators and open-source contributors who believed in something like Taichi before it was obviously worth believing in. Each of those encounters had a lot of randomness in it. If a few of them hadn't happened, I might have ended up on a very different path, and maybe I wouldn't have had the same energy at all.

Even the motivation itself is fragile. Being able to stay hungry assumes you're healthy, you're not overwhelmed by family or financial pressure, and you have enough small wins early on to believe effort pays off. That positive feedback loop is a kind of luck too. Some people work just as hard and get no feedback for years, and it's very hard to keep going in that situation.

So how do I deal with that? Two things. First, gratitude. Recognizing that luck helps me not take things for granted and not look down on people who didn't get the same breaks. Second, responsibility. If I was lucky enough to have this drive and these opportunities, then I'd better not waste them. Luck gives you the starting conditions; what you do with them is the part you can actually control. I try to focus my energy there, while staying humble about everything else.

r001.rationale: The response says staying hungry assumes being healthy, identifying physical condition as a possible basis for sustaining hard work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think luck is a huge part of it, and I try to be honest with myself about that. I was lucky to be born at a time when a kid could get a computer and teach themselves to program. I was lucky to have parents who didn't push me too hard in one direction. I was lucky to end up at MIT with advisors who gave me a lot of freedom, and I was lucky that Taichi came out at a moment when people suddenly cared about differentiable simulation and GPU programming in Python. If any of those things had been a little different, I'd probably be doing something else right now.

But here's how I actually use that understanding. When you realize how much of your position is luck, you feel a kind of debt. Not guilt, exactly, more like responsibility. A lot of people with more talent than me never got the same opportunities. So the hunger doesn't come from thinking I'm special. It comes from thinking, I got handed something, and the least I can do is not waste it.

The other thing is that luck is not evenly distributed over time. You get windows. The window where a new technology is immature and a small team can still make a difference, the window where you're young enough to work insane hours without your body complaining, the window where your advisors and collaborators happen to be in the same place. Those windows close. So when I feel lazy, I remind myself that the conditions that make my work possible right now are temporary, and nobody promised me they'd come back.

And honestly, working hard is also how you buy more lottery tickets. You can't control which one wins, but you can control how many you hold. Most of the things that went well for me, like open-sourcing Taichi or writing those early papers, I didn't know would matter. I just kept doing things, and some of them happened to land. So I'd say luck and hard work aren't opposites for me. Luck is what sets the game up, and hard work is how you show gratitude for being allowed to play.

r001.rationale: The response identifies being young enough to work long hours without physical complaints as a lucky, temporary condition that supports hard work.

astra-6.text:
I think luck plays a big role. Working hard can improve your chances, but it doesn’t mean you control the outcome. You can put a lot of effort into something and still need the right opportunity at the right time.

For me, recognizing that is actually a reason to stay hungry. If I’ve been fortunate enough to have an opportunity to do work I care about, I want to make good use of it. And when something works out, I try not to conclude that I’ve figured everything out. There’s still a lot to learn, and the next problem still takes effort.

r001.rationale: The response discusses luck, opportunities, and effort generally, but does not identify luck in Yuanming Hu’s physical condition as a foundation for sustaining hard work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve been very lucky, and recognizing that actually makes me want to work harder. A lot of things that made my work possible were not things I earned or controlled—the opportunities I had, the people I met, the timing. So I don’t think of hard work as proof that I deserve success. It’s more about making good use of those opportunities.

You can’t control whether every effort succeeds. But you can stay curious, keep trying, and be ready when an opportunity comes. For me, staying hungry is less about being dissatisfied with what I have and more about feeling that there are still interesting problems I want to solve.

r001.rationale: The response describes luck in opportunities, people, and timing, but does not identify Yuanming Hu’s physical condition as a possible basis for sustained hard work.
